title: The Humming Package Mystery
markdown:
Bakery Street tasted of sugar before breakfast and of spice by noon. Troubles that visited it were seldom dire. They were, more often, the sort that refused to sit still.

Ms. Gwendolyn Finch kept the post office, a giraffe of such height that her head tickled the shop awnings when she forgot to duck. She polished her spectacles each morning until each lens shone, as if a clear view might keep the day from wobbling. A postmistress, she believed, should look like a well-made cookie: tidy, finished, ready. True grace, she told herself while buffing, was not never making a mistake. It was smiling while you carried the mistake to its proper door.

Theo the hedgehog visited when the sealing-wax was warm. He had sensible prickles and quiet feet. The office smelled of paper and a little of honey, because someone had once posted a comb and the comb had opinions.

One sunny morning a package arrived that would not behave. It was no bigger than a teacup, and it hummed: a low, steady, tinkling hum that traveled up Finch's hooves like a hundred tiny bells trying to get out. The label, in bold shaky letters, said Urgent Delivery — Today Only. The name was Awen Grumbles, the baker whose frown could curdle milk and who disliked anything that made a cheerful sound.

Finch's long neck gave a small tremble. A humming box. For Awen. Today.

"This needs careful handling," she murmured, a low rumble meant only for the stamps. "No fuss. No noise. Poise."

Could another creature take it? Who would understand a box with a hobby? She decided, with the firmness of someone choosing the least embarrassing option, that she would deliver the riddle herself, and without a peep.

She set off, the box held carefully beneath her chin, neck tilted in what she hoped was dignity. The humming had other plans. It grew. It jingled down the street as if eager to share its music with everyone who had not asked.

Her first idea was muffling. A big fluffy baguette sat outside a bakery like a spare pillow. She dipped her head, graceful as a dip can be when you are mostly neck, and pressed the bread to the box.

The baguette boosted the melody. The jingle became a song. The bread, it seemed, was an instrument now.

"Just a small adjustment," she told a pigeon. The pigeon left at once, which was fair.

Next she balanced the box on the tip of her nose. Neck out, still as a statue of Postal Dedication. The wobbly perch and the happy tune were too much for even her practiced nerves. A twitch. The box tumbled, a little whirlwind of sound, and nudged a stack of Mrs. Gable's gingerbread men from a display cart. They fell like edible confetti, each with a soft thump and a spice that made the air briefly kinder.

Theo ambled closer. He watched Finch's elegant calm crack the way icing cracks on a cake that has cooled too fast. He knew she was trying to protect the street from Awen's famous temper. He also knew the street was already having a better morning than Awen usually allowed.

Finch did not give up. Giving up would have been a noise of its own.

"Perhaps," she said, neck asking the sky for a second opinion, "a louder sound is needed to cover the message."

She took a breath that started somewhere near her knees and hummed: not a polite hum, a deep cello of a hum, the kind a kind giant might use to soothe a mountain. Instead of quieting the box, the note walked over to old Mr. Pipkin's jam-jar tower and asked it to dance. The jars wobbled. They clattered. Bakery Street became a concert of good intentions.

Shoppers stopped. Bakers peeked. Children pointed at the tall giraffe whose spectacles had begun to slide. Finch's dignity felt less like polished china and more like a teacup with a chip you only notice when guests come.

Then the frown that started other frowns appeared. Awen Grumbles came out of his bakery, floury hands on his apron, brow furrowed like a ploughed field. He looked at the jingle as a man looks at an alarm clock that has chosen a hobby. Some trickster, his face said, was bothering him on purpose.

Finch gathered the package. Direct. Swift. End the noise before the baker's weather broke. She strode. Her long leg found a loose cobblestone that the charming street had been saving for exactly this. The box flew.

She shut her eyes. She waited for pottery, splintering, the famous rage.

The landing was a gentle clatter, a thud as if the box had only stretched. The lid sprang. The jangle, which had seemed so large a moment before, became a delicate tune, silver and a little shy. A music box. From a niece. Sent with the sort of hope that does not check a baker's mood first.

Finch opened one eye.

Awen had been walking like thunder. He stopped. The notes filled the floury air, sweet and faintly sad. His scowl, for the first time anyone present could remember, remembered how to soften. He looked at Finch not as a culprit but as a tall, crumb-dusted accident that had, somehow, finished the job.

Theo, from a safe spot, let out a small sigh that was mostly fondness.

Awen held the music box as if it might bruise. A shy smile arrived, a crack in a face that had practiced being closed. His niece came around the corner at a run, late and exactly on time, and saw the street still arranged around a song. She and Awen exchanged a nod that had more in it than bakery weather.

Finch stood among the fading notes, spectacles crooked, a dusting of baguette on her chin. Bakery Street smelled of gingerbread and jam and, underneath, of a delivery that had refused to be invisible. She did not polish the lenses just then. She left the smudge. The humming, at last, belonged to someone who had wanted it.
characters: Gwendolyn Finch (absent-minded giraffe postmistress), Theo (hedgehog friend), Awen Grumbles (grumpy baker)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
